edition: Issue 052: Australia hands Big Tech a bill it can't scroll past, Beauden Barrett 'reportedly' banks English rugby's biggest deal, and two 'retired' parakeets tell extinction to wait
tagline: Your 3-minute Thursday reset: a law that makes the algorithm the responsible adult, a man on 150 caps heading to Bristol on British money, and an endangered orange-fronted pair who gave the pension a rain check.

stories.headline: Australia passes an online safety law that could hit Big Tech with multibillion-dollar fines
stories.summary: Australia's Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care Act, exposing tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harm - following similar EU and UK laws, and landing as Christopher Luxon defends his own social media ban in front of a 15-year-old.

body.text: Australia's Parliament passed its Digital Duty of Care Act on Wednesday, a law that could expose the world's tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. Rather than reacting only after something goes wrong, it requires platforms to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it happens. The legislation is similar to the European Union's Digital Services Act of 2022 and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act of 2023, and both the United States and Australia's opposition have warned it would push companies into censoring lawful speech. It lands the same week New Zealand's own leader is under friendly fire over a proposed social media ban: Christopher Luxon defended the policy while being grilled by a 15-year-old in Christchurch.

Big Tech's favourite defence is the shoulder shrug: 'how could we possibly have foreseen the harm?' A position they hold only on days when they are not predicting exactly which advert will pause your scroll - at which point they can foresee everything about you except their own regulatory calendar. So Australia has done the sensible thing and started fining the shrugs, because multibillion-dollar penalties are the one language these companies demonstrably understand. And just to keep the symmetry honest, on the same side of the planet a prime minister has decided the answer to children's online lives is a ban he had to explain to an actual child - who did a better job of cross-examination than most parliamentary select committees. Somewhere between a law that makes the algorithm the responsible adult and a ban that a teenager picked apart in one sitting, there is the adult conversation a whole generation of politicians keeps scrolling past.

Stuff (26 Nov 2026, 'Australia passes online safety law, putting Big Tech at risk of multibillion-dollar fines'): Australia's Parliament on Wednesday passed the Digital Duty of Care Act, exposing tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms; the law requires platforms to proactively reduce risk before harm occurs. The US and the Australian opposition warned it would lead to censorship of lawful speech. It is similar to the EU's Digital Services Act (2022) and the UK's Online Safety Act (2023). In related coverage in the same report, Stuff showed National Party leader Christopher Luxon defending his proposed social media ban while fielding questions from a 15-year-old in Christchurch.

stories.headline: Beauden Barrett 'reportedly' signs one of English rugby's biggest ever deals with Bristol
stories.summary: The Times reports two-time World Rugby player of the year Beauden Barrett has signed a two-year deal with the Bristol Bears - one of the biggest deals in English rugby union history - departing after next year's World Cup, with Mail Sport earlier citing an offer worth more than NZ$4.7m.

body.text: Veteran All Black Beauden Barrett has reportedly signed a two-year deal with English club the Bristol Bears, according to The Times. The two-time World Rugby player of the year is expected to depart after next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia, in what The Times describes as one of the biggest deals in English rugby history. Earlier, Mail Sport reported Barrett had been offered a record-breaking package worth more than two million pounds (about NZ$4.7 million), though the final deal is understood to be less. An official announcement is expected after this weekend's final test of the year, when the All Blacks face England at Twickenham for a second consecutive week. Barrett, who played his 150th test last weekend, reportedly held lengthy talks with Bristol management while in London.

There is no more flexible word in world sport than 'reportedly' - it is doing a full aerobic workout here. A contract worth more than two million pounds, but actually less than that figure; one of the biggest deals in English rugby history, though the official announcement is still apparently waiting to be told it's happening. You could build a journalist's entire week on that much hedging, and somewhere a Bristol media manager is keeping their hand very, very still. But strip the qualifiers away and the line is simply: a man on 150 caps is heading north on money New Zealand could not find in a season, and English club rugby is about to make the biggest deal in its history around a veteran playmaker who couldn't stay past home. It is the eternal column about how the All Blacks lose their legends and the club game signs them - performed with an extra 'reportedly' for dramatic effect. Good luck over there, Beauden. Try not to let the British weather know how much they're paying you.

Stuff (26 Nov 2026, citing The Times and Mail Sport, 'All Black Beauden Barrett reportedly signs two-year deal with Bristol Bears'): Beauden Barrett has reportedly signed a two-year deal with the Bristol Bears, departing after next year's World Cup in Australia; The Times calls it one of the biggest deals in English rugby history. Mail Sport earlier reported a record-breaking offer of more than two million pounds (NZ$4.7m), with the final deal reportedly less. Barrett played his 150th test for the All Blacks last weekend and reportedly held lengthy talks with Bristol management while in London. An official announcement is expected after the All Blacks' final test of the year against England at Twickenham this weekend. Flag: this story rests on two report-based sources (The Times / Mail Sport) as relayed by Stuff; the deal is not yet officially confirmed as of writing, so the edition treats it as 'reportedly' rather than confirmed.

stories.headline: A pair of 'retired' critically endangered kākāriki karaka stun keepers with two surprise clutches
stories.summary: Sophia and Prince Polo, an aged pair of critically endangered kākāriki karaka officially 'retired' from breeding at Orana Wildlife Park, have produced a surprise clutch and then another four weeks later - a welcome boost for a bird twice declared extinct, with about 450 left.

body.text: An aged pair of critically endangered kākāriki karaka - the orange-fronted parakeet - has handed its species a surprise second wind at Christchurch's Orana Wildlife Park. Sophia and Prince Polo had been officially 'retired' from the breeding programme because of their age and moved to a display area. But Sophia, originally paired with a bird called Poldark, was re-paired with Prince Polo after Poldark died - and has since produced not one but two surprise clutches of eggs. The second clutch arrived just four weeks after the first, while her first babies were barely a month old, leaving keepers astonished. Native fauna manager Catherine Roughton put it simply: 'Prince Polo has clearly ignited something in her.'

The pair were 'retired' the way most of us would love to be retired - popped somewhere pretty, told the hard work is done, and left to enjoy the view. Except these two decided, mid-pension, that a critically endangered population with about 450 members did not actually have the luxury of knocking off early. And what a way to clock back in: one clutch, then - four weeks later, with month-old chicks in the nest - another. Keepers thought they had seen everything; Sophia decided they had seen two of everything. It is even sweeter knowing this is a bird that has been officially declared extinct twice, which is a comeback arc not even a streaming series manages, and that these particular chicks carry genetics from wild nests collected eight years ago - meaning a small retirement fling just became the recovery programme's headline act. Somewhere a display-area sign saying 'retired' should probably be updated to 'consultant emeritus, absolutely not done'. Congratulations to Prince Polo on the igniting.

RNZ (26 Nov 2026, 'Retired' pair of critically endangered kākāriki karaka stun keepers with two sets of eggs): an aged pair of orange-fronted parakeets, Sophia and Prince Polo, officially retired from breeding and moved to a display area at Orana Wildlife Park, produced an unexpected clutch of eggs and then, four weeks later, a second clutch while the first chicks were a month old. Sophia was originally paired with a bird called Poldark and re-paired with Prince Polo after Poldark died. Native fauna manager Catherine Roughton said Prince Polo was now feeding his four-month-old babies and had 'clearly ignited something in her'. The kākāriki karaka has twice been declared extinct; about 450 are estimated to remain, mostly on offshore islands or at the Brook Waimarama Sanctuary near Nelson, with a small remnant population in Canterbury. DOC kākāriki karaka recovery programme lead Wayne Beggs said the pair were collected as eggs from wild nests in the Poulter Valley about eight years ago and each clutch holds important genetics for the captive-breeding and wild-release programme.
